full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] Vision pretraining budgets are routinely allocated using intuitions imported from language-model scaling work (Chinchilla-style token-parameter balance), but images are not tokens and vision datasets have different redundancy structure.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The compute-optimal frontier for contrastive/self-supervised vision encoders is systematically more data-hungry per parameter than the language frontier because per-image information content after augmentation is lower than per-token information in text, and the vision-specific ratio is stable enough across two orders of magnitude of compute to serve as an allocation rule.

full_record.why_important: Every vision foundation model release implicitly bets millions of dollars of compute on an allocation heuristic that has never been fitted for vision; a fitted rule would either correct or validate that bet.

full_record.main_risk: The compute-optimal ratio may itself depend on the pretraining objective and augmentation recipe, so a single fitted rule may not generalize beyond the tested recipe family.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Practitioners assume language-derived parameter-data balance intuitions transfer to vision with minor correction, or ignore the question and scale both together.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: Augmentation may raise the effective information per image enough that vision is actually less data-hungry than language at matched compute, inverting the predicted direction.

full_record.one_line_idea: Input resolution is a third scaling axis with its own exponent, and vision loss is better modeled as L(params, data, resolution) than by folding resolution into compute.
full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] Vision scaling studies treat resolution as a preprocessing detail or a fine-tuning trick, yet resolution changes both FLOPs and the information available per image, confounding fitted parameter and data exponents.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Downstream error follows a separable three-term power law in parameters, unique images, and training resolution, with a resolution exponent that is task-dependent but model-size-independent, because resolution controls information supply per sample rather than model capacity.
full_record.falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Adding a resolution term to a two-term scaling fit will reduce held-out prediction error of downstream accuracy by at least 25% relative on a grid spanning 96px-384px, with the fitted resolution exponent stable within +/-30% across model sizes; the idea is falsified if the three-term fit improves held-out prediction by under 10% or the resolution exponent varies by more than 2x across model sizes.
full_record.why_important: If resolution has its own stable exponent, pretraining budget planning can trade resolution against data and parameters analytically instead of by folklore, and dense-task practitioners get a principled way to anticipate high-resolution gains.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Resolution ablations exist in many papers, but a jointly fitted three-axis scaling law with a pre-registered held-out prediction criterion appears missing for vision.
full_record.minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a factorial grid over 3 model sizes x 4 data sizes x 4 resolutions on public data with a fixed recipe, fit two-term and three-term laws on 80% of the grid, and compare extrapolation error on the held-out corner cells.
full_record.main_risk: Patchification interacts with resolution (token count changes), so the resolution effect may be an architecture artifact of ViTs rather than a data-information law; running a small CNN control adds cost.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Resolution is widely treated as a fine-tuning-time knob or a fixed constant, not a first-class scaling variable with its own exponent.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: Resolution gains may be entirely mediated by token count, making the resolution term redundant with a compute term and the three-term law an overparameterized refit.

full_record.why_important: It redirects dense-prediction practitioners from chasing bigger backbones to cheaper token-count scaling, and it corrects scaling-law fits that use parameters as the sole capacity variable.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Patch-size ablations exist, but a variance-decomposition of dense-transfer scaling into token-count versus parameter-count contributions with a pre-registered ratio appears untested.

full_record.main_risk: Token count and parameters interact through optimization stability, so some grid corners may undertrain and bias the variance decomposition.

full_record.why_important: If final checkpoints are not the best transfer artifacts, checkpoint-selection policy for released foundation models is leaving transfer performance on the table, and data-constrained labs are actively hurting themselves by training longer.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Ossification is described in language transfer scaling (Hernandez et al.); a controlled vision version with per-budget fine-tuning curves and a checkpoint-selection recommendation appears missing.

full_record.main_risk: The effect may only appear under heavy repetition of a small corpus and vanish at web-scale unique-data regimes, limiting relevance for frontier models while remaining relevant for domain-specific pretraining.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] More pretraining is assumed at worst neutral for downstream fine-tuning; final checkpoints are shipped by default.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern augmentation and weight decay may prevent representation overfitting entirely, making downstream performance genuinely monotone in pretraining compute.

one_line_idea: Parameter scaling and data scaling buy different error components in dense transfer: data buys semantic coverage, parameters buy localization precision, and the two are separable by error taxonomy at matched upstream loss.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] At matched upstream loss, models that got there with more data make fewer semantic errors (misclassification, missed rare categories) while models that got there with more parameters make fewer geometric errors (poor box localization, imprecise keypoints), because data supplies concept coverage while capacity supplies function-fitting precision.

full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] Scaling analyses collapse model quality to a scalar (loss or a single accuracy), so two checkpoints with equal upstream loss are treated as interchangeable even when reached by different parameter-data routes.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] At matched upstream loss, models that got there with more data make fewer semantic errors (misclassification, missed rare categories) while models that got there with more parameters make fewer geometric errors (poor box localization, imprecise keypoints), because data supplies concept coverage while capacity supplies function-fitting precision.

full_record.why_important: It breaks the equivalence class assumed by loss-matched scaling analysis and gives dense-task practitioners a principled rule for which scaling axis to buy given their dominant error mode.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Loss-matched comparisons across scaling routes exist for language perplexity trade-offs; an error-taxonomy dissociation for vision dense transfer appears untested.

full_record.main_risk: Exactly matching upstream loss across routes requires careful schedule tuning, and residual loss differences could masquerade as route effects.

full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: Localization precision may be set almost entirely by token resolution rather than parameters, collapsing the predicted dissociation into a resolution artifact.

one_line_idea: The native-resolution distribution of the pretraining corpus imprints a scale prior on encoders: models systematically underperform at object scales rare in their corpus, and resolution-mix reshaping moves the failure profile predictably.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Despite resize normalization, the distribution of object-scale-in-pixels in the corpus imprints a prior: recognition and localization accuracy as a function of test-time object scale mirrors the training-time scale histogram, and reshaping the corpus scale mix shifts the accuracy-versus-scale profile in the corresponding direction.

full_record.one_line_idea: The native-resolution distribution of the pretraining corpus imprints a scale prior on encoders: models systematically underperform at object scales rare in their corpus, and resolution-mix reshaping moves the failure profile predictably.
full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] Corpora mix images of very different native resolutions and object scales, then training pipelines resize everything to fixed input sizes; the surviving effect of the original scale distribution on model behavior is unexamined.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Despite resize normalization, the distribution of object-scale-in-pixels in the corpus imprints a prior: recognition and localization accuracy as a function of test-time object scale mirrors the training-time scale histogram, and reshaping the corpus scale mix shifts the accuracy-versus-scale profile in the corresponding direction.
full_record.falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Encoders pretrained on scale-mix-reshaped corpora (small-object-enriched versus large-object-enriched, matched size and content) will show opposite-signed accuracy differences of at least 4 points at the extreme test-scale bins, with profile shifts tracking the training histograms; the idea is falsified if the accuracy-versus-scale profiles differ by under 1.5 points everywhere despite the histogram intervention.
full_record.why_important: It reveals a composition variable that survives preprocessing and explains persistent scale-dependent failures, and it offers a data-level fix (scale-mix reshaping) that no augmentation currently targets deliberately.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Scale augmentation is standard, but the claim that corpus-level object-scale composition leaves a measurable prior after standard augmentation, with a controlled reshaping test, appears new territory.
full_record.minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate object-scale histograms on a public corpus with a detector, build reshaped resamples, pretrain matched small encoders with identical augmentation, and evaluate accuracy versus test-time object scale on held-out data.
full_record.main_risk: Standard multi-scale crop augmentation may genuinely erase the corpus prior, yielding a null that is informative but less publishable.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Resize-and-crop augmentation is assumed to fully decouple model behavior from the corpus scale distribution.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: The imprint may exist but be too small to matter next to augmentation effects, making it a curiosity rather than a design lever.
full_record.fastest_falsification_experiment: 2-3 small pretrains on reshaped public subsets plus scale-stratified evaluation, one A100: about 4 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Concept drift of the visual world is fittable as a per-year decay law: models pretrained on older real crawls lose accuracy on newer-world probes at a measurable rate, giving corpora a quantifiable shelf life.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Accuracy on time-stamped probes decays approximately linearly-in-log-time with the gap between crawl vintage and probe vintage, with a decay constant that varies by category dynamism (fast for products/interfaces, near zero for natural kinds), so corpus vintage composition can be planned like depreciation.

full_record.one_line_idea: Concept drift of the visual world is fittable as a per-year decay law: models pretrained on older real crawls lose accuracy on newer-world probes at a measurable rate, giving corpora a quantifiable shelf life.
full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] Pretraining corpora are snapshots of the visual world at crawl time (products, vehicles, fashion, interfaces change), yet corpus age is absent from scaling and composition analysis, and models are deployed for years.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Accuracy on time-stamped probes decays approximately linearly-in-log-time with the gap between crawl vintage and probe vintage, with a decay constant that varies by category dynamism (fast for products/interfaces, near zero for natural kinds), so corpus vintage composition can be planned like depreciation.
full_record.falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Pretraining matched models on real crawl slices from different years and probing with year-stamped test sets will show a monotone vintage-gap effect of at least 3 accuracy points per 5 years on dynamic categories and under 1 point on static categories; the idea is falsified if vintage effects are under 1 point per 5 years on dynamic categories or non-monotone in gap.
full_record.why_important: It prices data freshness against data volume for corpus maintenance, telling builders when refreshing beats growing and which categories drive the need.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Temporal robustness studies exist for classifiers on shifting test sets; a vintage-controlled pretraining intervention with fitted per-category decay constants appears missing.
full_record.minimal_falsification_experiment: Use a public corpus with upload timestamps (e.g., YFCC-style) to build year-sliced training sets, pretrain matched small models, and evaluate on year-stamped probes spanning dynamic and static categories.
full_record.main_risk: Older crawl slices differ in camera quality and resolution, confounding vintage with image statistics; quality-matched controls are required.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Corpus age is treated as irrelevant next to corpus size; refreshes happen for legal and availability reasons, not modeled performance decay.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: Most benchmark and deployment content may be temporally stable enough that decay constants are negligible outside narrow product domains.
full_record.fastest_falsification_experiment: 4 small pretrains on year-sliced public data plus stamped probes, one A100: about 4-5 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: People-image share has decoupled utility and privacy curves: person-task transfer saturates at a modest share while memorization of individuals keeps rising, so current corpora sit past the utility knee but still on the risk ramp.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Transfer to person-centric tasks (pose, attribute recognition) saturates in people-image share well below typical web levels, while per-individual memorization signal (re-identification of repeated individuals from embeddings) continues growing with share, creating a regime where share reduction is privacy-positive and utility-neutral.

full_record.one_line_idea: People-image share has decoupled utility and privacy curves: person-task transfer saturates at a modest share while memorization of individuals keeps rising, so current corpora sit past the utility knee but still on the risk ramp.
full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] Web corpora contain large fractions of images with people, chosen by crawl accident; person-centric task performance and person-level privacy risk both depend on this share, but the two response curves have never been measured together.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Transfer to person-centric tasks (pose, attribute recognition) saturates in people-image share well below typical web levels, while per-individual memorization signal (re-identification of repeated individuals from embeddings) continues growing with share, creating a regime where share reduction is privacy-positive and utility-neutral.
full_record.falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Sweeping people-image share across 10%, 25%, and 50% at matched corpus size will change pose-transfer PCK by under 2 points between 25% and 50%, while individual re-identification success from embeddings rises by at least 30% relative over the same interval; the idea is falsified if utility keeps climbing materially (over 4 points) to 50% share or re-identification stays flat.
full_record.why_important: It would give corpus builders an evidence-based people-share target that preserves capability while measurably reducing person-level risk, a rare free lunch in privacy.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Face-obfuscation studies measured utility effects of blurring; the joint share-sweep of utility and individual-memorization curves appears unmeasured.
full_record.minimal_falsification_experiment: Build share-controlled resamples of a public corpus (person detector for tagging), pretrain small encoders, evaluate pose/attribute transfer, and run embedding-based re-identification probes on individuals repeated in training versus controls.
full_record.main_risk: Re-identification probes need individuals with multiple photos in the corpus and held-out photos for testing, which constrains dataset choice and may limit statistical power.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] More people data is assumed necessary for person-task quality, and privacy risk is treated as an orthogonal compliance issue rather than a curve to be traded against a saturating utility curve.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: Person-task transfer may not saturate when downstream tasks include fine-grained interaction understanding, keeping utility on the ramp alongside risk.
full_record.fastest_falsification_experiment: 3 small pretrains plus transfer and re-identification probes on public data, one A100: about 5 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Contextual bias is a dose-dependent function of co-occurrence statistics in pretraining data: resampling rare-context images measurably improves out-of-context recognition at a fittable exchange rate.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Out-of-context failure rate is a smooth decreasing function of the count of decorrelated exemplars (object appearing outside its typical context) in pretraining, so corpus-level resampling that raises rare-context counts buys out-of-context accuracy at a measurable per-example exchange rate without hurting in-context accuracy.

full_record.one_line_idea: Contextual bias is a dose-dependent function of co-occurrence statistics in pretraining data: resampling rare-context images measurably improves out-of-context recognition at a fittable exchange rate.
full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] Models rely on context (cows on grass, keyboards near monitors) and fail on out-of-context instances; the reliance is usually attributed to architecture or objective rather than quantified against the co-occurrence statistics of the training corpus.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Out-of-context failure rate is a smooth decreasing function of the count of decorrelated exemplars (object appearing outside its typical context) in pretraining, so corpus-level resampling that raises rare-context counts buys out-of-context accuracy at a measurable per-example exchange rate without hurting in-context accuracy.
full_record.falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Increasing rare-context exemplar share for 20 tracked categories by 4x (matched total size) will reduce out-of-context error on those categories by at least 15% relative with in-context error changing by under 3% relative; the idea is falsified if out-of-context error improves under 5% relative or in-context error degrades by more than the out-of-context gain.
full_record.why_important: It reframes a robustness pathology as a controllable composition dose, giving a data-level alternative to architectural debiasing methods and a way to budget for it.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Contextual-bias phenomena are established; the controlled co-occurrence-resampling dose-response at matched corpus size appears missing.
full_record.minimal_falsification_experiment: Tag object-context pairs on a public corpus, build resamples with boosted rare-context counts for tracked categories, pretrain small models, and evaluate in-context versus out-of-context recognition on held-out stress sets.
full_record.main_risk: Rare-context images in web data are rare in absolute terms, capping the achievable boost and possibly requiring category choice to follow data availability.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Context reliance is treated as an inductive-bias problem to be fixed by methods, not as a corpus co-occurrence dose to be adjusted.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: Context reliance may be driven by the downstream task data rather than pretraining statistics, making pretraining resampling ineffective.
full_record.fastest_falsification_experiment: 3 small pretrains on resampled public data plus stress evaluation, one A100: about 4 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Vision pretraining tolerates far more data repetition than language lore implies: the per-epoch effective-data decay constant is small under strong augmentation, and the unique-data premium has been overstated for vision.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Under standard crop/color augmentation, the value decay per repetition in vision is governed by augmentation entropy: with strong augmentation, repeated epochs retain most of the marginal value of fresh data for many more repetitions than language-derived intuitions predict, and the decay constant is measurable and augmentation-dependent.

full_record.one_line_idea: Vision pretraining tolerates far more data repetition than language lore implies: the per-epoch effective-data decay constant is small under strong augmentation, and the unique-data premium has been overstated for vision.
full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] Language-model results on data-constrained scaling (repeating data loses value rapidly after a few epochs) are imported into vision planning, but augmentation makes vision epochs non-identical in ways language epochs are not.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Under standard crop/color augmentation, the value decay per repetition in vision is governed by augmentation entropy: with strong augmentation, repeated epochs retain most of the marginal value of fresh data for many more repetitions than language-derived intuitions predict, and the decay constant is measurable and augmentation-dependent.
full_record.falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] At matched total samples seen, a corpus repeated 8x with strong augmentation will retain at least 80% of the probe-accuracy gain of an 8x-larger unique corpus, versus under 60% with weak augmentation; the idea is falsified if strong-augmentation retention falls below 65% (vision behaves like language lore) or augmentation fails to modulate retention by at least 10 points.
full_record.why_important: Data-constrained domains (medical, industrial, scientific) need to know whether to spend on collection or compute; a measured vision-specific repetition law directly prices that decision.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Data-constrained scaling laws are quantified for language (Muennighoff et al.); the vision analogue with augmentation as the controlling variable appears unmeasured.
full_record.minimal_falsification_experiment: Cross unique-data size against repetition factor at matched samples seen, under two augmentation strengths, pretrain small encoders, and fit effective-data retention per repetition.
full_record.main_risk: Retention may depend on the pretraining objective family, requiring at least two objectives to claim generality and doubling the run count.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Repeating data more than a few epochs is widely assumed to be nearly worthless relative to fresh data, importing language-model findings wholesale.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: Augmentation may add diversity that is irrelevant to the features that saturate, making vision repetition decay match language decay after all.
full_record.fastest_falsification_experiment: About 12 small pretrains on public subsets, one A100: about 4 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Augmentation is a data multiplier with a scale-decaying exchange rate: its effective-dataset-size factor is large for small models and shrinks predictably with model scale, so augmentation-heavy recipes are a small-model subsidy.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Augmentation multiplies effective dataset size by a factor that decays with model scale because large models trained on abundant data already internalize the invariances augmentation teaches, so the augmentation-optimal strength falls along a fittable curve in (model size, data size).

full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Augmentation multiplies effective dataset size by a factor that decays with model scale because large models trained on abundant data already internalize the invariances augmentation teaches, so the augmentation-optimal strength falls along a fittable curve in (model size, data size).
full_record.falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The fitted effective-data multiplier of a fixed augmentation policy will shrink by at least 40% when model scale grows 10x at abundant data, and the accuracy-optimal augmentation strength will fall monotonically with scale across a 3-point grid; the idea is falsified if the multiplier shrinks under 15% or optimal strength is scale-invariant.
full_record.why_important: It explains recurring anecdotes of augmentation mattering less for big models, and it converts augmentation tuning at scale from re-search into extrapolation along a fitted curve.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Augmentation-versus-data-size interactions have been studied at small scale; the effective-multiplier decay law across model scale appears unfitted.
full_record.minimal_falsification_experiment: Grid model size against augmentation strength at two data sizes, measure probe accuracy, fit the effective-data multiplier per cell by matching against a no-augmentation data-size sweep, and test the decay trend.
full_record.main_risk: The multiplier depends on which invariances the probe suite rewards, so multiple probe families are needed to avoid overclaiming from one metric.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Augmentation recipes validated at moderate scale are assumed to transfer to larger scales with unchanged benefit.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: For dense-task transfer, augmentation may encode invariances that models never learn from data alone, keeping the multiplier scale-stable for those uses.
full_record.fastest_falsification_experiment: About 20 small pretrains on public subsets, one A100: about 5 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Targeted repetition beats uniform repetition: oversampling tail-concept images when repeating a fixed corpus recovers a large share of the benefit of new tail data, at zero collection cost.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The marginal value of a repetition is largest for under-represented, under-fit content, so frequency-aware oversampling of tail concepts during repeated epochs improves tail performance substantially at fixed samples seen while leaving head performance within noise, outperforming uniform repetition overall.

full_record.one_line_idea: Targeted repetition beats uniform repetition: oversampling tail-concept images when repeating a fixed corpus recovers a large share of the benefit of new tail data, at zero collection cost.
full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] When corpora are repeated for multiple epochs, every image is repeated equally, although marginal value per repetition plausibly differs enormously between over-represented head content and under-fit tail content.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The marginal value of a repetition is largest for under-represented, under-fit content, so frequency-aware oversampling of tail concepts during repeated epochs improves tail performance substantially at fixed samples seen while leaving head performance within noise, outperforming uniform repetition overall.
full_record.falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] At matched samples seen, tail-oversampled repetition will improve tail-concept probe accuracy by at least 3 points versus uniform repetition with head accuracy within 0.5 points, and will recover at least 40% of the tail gain achievable by actually adding new tail data of the same count; the idea is falsified if tail gains are under 1 point or head losses exceed tail gains.
full_record.why_important: It is an immediately deployable, collection-free improvement to every data-constrained pretraining run, with the recovered-fraction number quantifying how far sampling policy can substitute for data acquisition.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Class-balanced sampling is standard in supervised long-tail learning; its formulation as a repetition-policy law for pretraining corpora with a new-data-equivalence measurement appears missing.
full_record.minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate concept frequencies on a public corpus, pretrain matched models under uniform versus tail-oversampled repetition at fixed samples seen, plus a fresh-tail-data reference arm, and compare stratified probe results.
full_record.main_risk: Aggressive tail oversampling amplifies memorization and label-noise effects on exactly the repeated items, potentially trading privacy risk for accuracy (measurable within the same runs).
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Epoch repetition is treated as uniform by default; sampling policy attention goes to filtering, not to repetition allocation.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: Tail underperformance may reflect irreducible visual ambiguity rather than under-fitting, in which case extra repetitions buy memorization instead of generalization.
full_record.fastest_falsification_experiment: 3 small pretrains plus stratified probes on public data, one A100: about 4 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Epochs buy fit, unique data buys coverage: repetition and fresh data improve dissociable error components, and the decomposition predicts which failure modes more epochs can and cannot fix.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] At matched samples seen, unique-data runs specifically win on coverage-limited components (rare concepts, unusual contexts, tail slices) while repetition matches them on fit-limited components (head-class margins, common-case robustness), because repetition cannot add support to unsampled regions.

full_record.one_line_idea: Epochs buy fit, unique data buys coverage: repetition and fresh data improve dissociable error components, and the decomposition predicts which failure modes more epochs can and cannot fix.
full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] Matched-samples-seen comparisons between repeated and unique data report aggregate accuracy differences, leaving unexplained what kind of performance the unique-data premium consists of.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] At matched samples seen, unique-data runs specifically win on coverage-limited components (rare concepts, unusual contexts, tail slices) while repetition matches them on fit-limited components (head-class margins, common-case robustness), because repetition cannot add support to unsampled regions.

full_record.why_important: It converts the vague more-unique-data-is-better belief into an actionable diagnosis: teams whose failures are head-case failures can stop paying for fresh data, and vice versa.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The aggregate repetition penalty is documented in data-constrained scaling work; its decomposition into coverage-versus-fit components appears untested.
full_record.minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain matched pairs (unique versus 8x-repeated at equal samples seen), evaluate frequency-stratified and context-stratified probe suites, and decompose the gap.
full_record.main_risk: Stratification depends on frequency estimates from imperfect taggers, so slice boundaries carry noise that must be bootstrapped.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Fresh data is assumed generically better without a component-level account of what it buys.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: Repetition may also lose head-case robustness through memorization-induced overconfidence, spreading the gap across all slices.
full_record.fastest_falsification_experiment: 2 small pretrains plus stratified evaluation on public data, one A100: about 3 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Aggressive near-duplicate removal hurts fine-grained recognition: near-duplicates of the same instance are free hard positives, and the dedup-threshold optimum is task-dependent rather than universal.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Near-duplicate groups (same object under small pose, lighting, or crop changes) function as naturally occurring hard-positive pairs that teach fine-grained invariance, so tightening dedup thresholds degrades fine-grained and instance-level tasks while leaving coarse recognition unchanged, making the optimal threshold a task-weighted choice.

full_record.why_important: Dedup policy is applied to every serious corpus and is currently justified by storage, efficiency, and privacy arguments alone; a measured utility cost on specific task families changes how thresholds should be set and reported.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Dedup-improves-training results exist at coarse granularity; the fine-grained-cost side of the curve with a task-dependent optimum appears unmeasured.

full_record.main_risk: Matched-final-size construction means arms differ in content beyond duplication, requiring careful sampling so removed duplicates are replaced by content-matched singletons.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] More deduplication is assumed at worst neutral and generally good for training efficiency and generalization.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: Contrastive objectives may treat near-duplicates as trivial positives that contribute nothing, making their removal genuinely free even for fine-grained tasks.

full_record.one_line_idea: Attribute-object binding emerges only when pretraining data decorrelates attributes from objects: binding capability tracks the count of counter-stereotypical pairings, not total data, and can be induced early by decorrelation-targeted resampling.
full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] Vision-language models notoriously fail attribute binding (confusing which object carries which color or material), and the failure persists across scale in an irregular way that scale-centric accounts do not explain.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Binding competence is gated by exposure to attribute-object combinations that break natural correlations (yellow bananas teach nothing about binding; blue bananas do), so the capability tracks counter-stereotypical pair counts, and resampling real data to raise decorrelation moves binding scores at fixed total scale.

full_record.why_important: Binding is a canonical unsolved compositionality failure; establishing it as a data-decorrelation dose effect redirects effort from architecture search to targeted real-data sourcing and forecasts which corpora can never teach binding.

one_line_idea: Augmentation strength buys privacy at a measurable exchange rate: stronger cropping and color jitter suppress per-image memorization with a fittable privacy-utility frontier, and some augmentation regimes are strictly dominant.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Augmentation reduces memorization by preventing the model from anchoring on exact pixel configurations, with a dose-dependent suppression that is steeper than its utility cost over a wide range, producing a frontier with a wide near-free privacy zone and identifiable dominated policies.

full_record.one_line_idea: Augmentation strength buys privacy at a measurable exchange rate: stronger cropping and color jitter suppress per-image memorization with a fittable privacy-utility frontier, and some augmentation regimes are strictly dominant.
full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] Augmentation policies are tuned exclusively for accuracy, while anecdotal evidence suggests augmentation also disrupts verbatim memorization; the joint frontier has never been mapped for vision encoders.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Augmentation reduces memorization by preventing the model from anchoring on exact pixel configurations, with a dose-dependent suppression that is steeper than its utility cost over a wide range, producing a frontier with a wide near-free privacy zone and identifiable dominated policies.
full_record.falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Sweeping augmentation strength over 5 levels will reduce panel membership AUC by at least 0.15 between weakest and strongest while probe accuracy varies non-monotonically, and at least one policy pair will show strict dominance (better on both axes); the idea is falsified if membership AUC varies by under 0.05 across the sweep (augmentation is privacy-irrelevant) or privacy gains map one-to-one onto utility losses (no free zone).
full_record.why_important: If augmentation is a cheap privacy lever, privacy-conscious training gains a zero-infrastructure mitigation, and augmentation policy debates acquire a second axis that changes existing recommendations.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Augmentation-versus-memorization interactions are noted in passing in SSL memorization work; a mapped privacy-utility frontier with dominance analysis appears missing.
full_record.minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain matched encoders under 5 augmentation policies with an injected panel, measure membership AUC and a fixed utility suite per policy, and plot the frontier.
full_record.main_risk: Augmentation may suppress the specific attack used while leaving other extraction channels open, overstating privacy gains; multiple attack families are required.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Privacy protection is assumed to require dedicated mechanisms (private optimizers, data exclusion), with augmentation seen purely as an accuracy tool.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: Strong augmentation may push memorization into augmentation-invariant features rather than removing it, changing its form but not its magnitude.
full_record.fastest_falsification_experiment: 5 small pretrains plus attacks and probes on public data, one A100: about 5-6 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Encoders memorize background people: individuals occupying under 5% of image pixels are re-identifiable from embeddings of held-out photos, and selective face/person blurring of the corpus removes the risk at near-zero utility cost.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Encoders bind identity features of repeatedly appearing individuals even when those individuals are small and incidental, so embedding-space retrieval links held-out photos of such individuals to their training appearances well above chance, and this linkage is eliminated by corpus-side person-region blurring with negligible effect on standard transfer.

full_record.one_line_idea: Encoders memorize background people: individuals occupying under 5% of image pixels are re-identifiable from embeddings of held-out photos, and selective face/person blurring of the corpus removes the risk at near-zero utility cost.
full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] Web images contain incidental bystanders, and corpus-level face blurring has been shown to cost little accuracy on ImageNet-scale supervised training; whether unblurred incidental people are actually memorized by modern encoders in a re-identifiable way is unmeasured.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Encoders bind identity features of repeatedly appearing individuals even when those individuals are small and incidental, so embedding-space retrieval links held-out photos of such individuals to their training appearances well above chance, and this linkage is eliminated by corpus-side person-region blurring with negligible effect on standard transfer.
full_record.falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] For individuals appearing 10 or more times as sub-5%-area bystanders in training, held-out-photo retrieval will rank their training contexts in the top 1% of the gallery at least 5x more often than for matched non-training individuals, and blurred-corpus controls will reduce this to under 1.5x with probe-suite utility change under 0.5 points; the idea is falsified if bystander linkage is under 2x chance in the unblurred condition (no incidental memorization) or blurring costs over 2 points of utility.
full_record.why_important: It tests the exact privacy claim regulators care about (are people in the background of web photos extractable from released encoders) and evaluates the practical mitigation in the same experiment.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Face-blurring utility costs are measured for supervised ImageNet training; the incidental-person memorization measurement and blurring-as-mitigation test for modern SSL encoders appear missing.
full_record.minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct a corpus with tracked repeated bystanders (public photo collections with identity metadata), pretrain encoders on raw versus person-blurred variants, and run cross-photo identity retrieval plus a utility suite.
full_record.main_risk: Public datasets with repeated identifiable bystanders and consent-appropriate licensing are limited; celebrity-in-crowd photo collections may be the only viable substrate.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Incidental background people are assumed too small and rare to be memorized, so blurring is framed as an abundance of caution with a feared utility cost.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: Sub-5%-area appearances may fall below the resolution at which identity features survive patchification, making incidental memorization physically negligible.
full_record.fastest_falsification_experiment: 2 small pretrains plus retrieval and probes on public data, one A100: about 5 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Structured outputs leak more: membership inference against dense predictors using spatially resolved error patterns beats pooled image-level attacks by a wide margin, because per-location residuals carry per-image fingerprints.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Training on an image leaves spatially structured residual patterns (which regions the model fits unusually well) that survive in dense predictions, so attacks that use the spatial residual field as a signature outperform pooled-loss attacks substantially, making dense models strictly leakier than their classification counterparts at matched training.

full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] Membership inference methodology was developed for classifiers with scalar outputs, and is applied to dense models by pooling losses over space, discarding exactly the high-dimensional structure dense models expose.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Training on an image leaves spatially structured residual patterns (which regions the model fits unusually well) that survive in dense predictions, so attacks that use the spatial residual field as a signature outperform pooled-loss attacks substantially, making dense models strictly leakier than their classification counterparts at matched training.
full_record.falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On matched depth-estimation and classification models trained on the same images, a spatial-residual-field attack will exceed pooled-loss attack AUC by at least 0.08 on the dense model, and the dense model's best-attack AUC will exceed the classifier's by at least 0.05; the idea is falsified if spatial structure adds under 0.02 AUC or dense models prove no leakier than classifiers.
full_record.why_important: Dense models are deployed in privacy-sensitive settings (driving, medical, mapping) under auditing standards developed on classifiers; if dense outputs are structurally leakier, those standards understate risk categorically.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Membership inference against segmentation exists in scattered work; the spatial-residual-signature formulation with a dense-versus-classifier leakage comparison appears undeveloped.
full_record.minimal_falsification_experiment: Train depth and classification models on the same public image set, implement pooled and spatial-field attacks (residual autocorrelation, per-region ranking features), and compare AUCs under matched threat models.
full_record.main_risk: Spatial attacks need ground-truth or proxy targets at test time; attacks must be designed for the realistic setting where the attacker lacks true labels.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Dense models are implicitly assumed to inherit classifier-level membership risk, with output structure treated as irrelevant to leakage.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense training averages gradients over many spatial locations per image, which may dilute per-image fingerprints below what spatial attacks can recover.
full_record.fastest_falsification_experiment: 2 trainings plus attack implementation on public data (NYUv2, ImageNet subset), one A100: about 4 GPU-days; depth-error and logit signals only.

full_record.why_important: Foundation-model privacy auditing currently belongs to whoever can afford shadow fleets; a validated cheap substitute makes independent auditing feasible for regulators, journalists, and academics.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Difficulty normalization via shadow models is standard; substituting corpus-statistics-based difficulty and quantifying recovered power appears untested for vision encoders.

full_record.main_risk: Data-level difficulty may correlate poorly with model-specific fitting noise for mid-difficulty examples, capping recovery below the useful threshold.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Strong membership attacks are believed to require shadow training as an essential ingredient, making foundation-scale audits impractical by definition.

one_line_idea: Membership signals transfer across models trained on overlapping crawls: an attack fitted on a small open encoder identifies members of a large closed encoder's corpus, because web-crawl overlap makes membership a property of the image, not the model.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Because web-crawl corpora share the high-duplication head of the image web, per-image membership scores computed against open encoders correlate strongly with membership in closed models' corpora, enabling cross-model membership auditing without access to the target's training details.

full_record.one_line_idea: Membership signals transfer across models trained on overlapping crawls: an attack fitted on a small open encoder identifies members of a large closed encoder's corpus, because web-crawl overlap makes membership a property of the image, not the model.
full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] Closed foundation encoders are trained on undisclosed crawls that heavily overlap public crawls, and auditors have no attack normalization path against closed models.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Because web-crawl corpora share the high-duplication head of the image web, per-image membership scores computed against open encoders correlate strongly with membership in closed models' corpora, enabling cross-model membership auditing without access to the target's training details.
full_record.falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Membership scores from an open encoder will predict membership in a second, independently trained encoder's corpus (simulating the closed target, with controlled crawl overlap of 60-80%) with AUC at least 0.70 on the overlapping stratum; the idea is falsified if cross-model AUC falls below 0.58, showing membership signals are model-specific even under heavy corpus overlap.
full_record.why_important: It would establish that closed-model privacy cannot hide behind corpus secrecy where crawls overlap, giving auditors and litigants a scientifically grounded inference path.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Attack transferability is studied across architectures on identical training sets; transfer across partially overlapping corpora as an auditing primitive appears unformalized.
full_record.minimal_falsification_experiment: Train pairs of encoders on corpora with controlled overlap fractions, fit attacks on one, evaluate membership prediction for the other stratified by overlap status, and map transfer AUC versus overlap.
full_record.main_risk: Transfer may be driven almost entirely by duplication-heavy head content, making the auditable stratum small and legally less interesting.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Membership inference is assumed to require attack access fitted to the specific target model and its data distribution.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: Idiosyncratic training choices (augmentation, mixture weights) may decorrelate per-image signals across models enough to destroy transfer.
full_record.fastest_falsification_experiment: 4 small pretrains with controlled overlap plus attacks, one A100: about 5 GPU-days on public data.

one_line_idea: Distilled students inherit their teacher's membership secrets: distillation on disjoint transfer data still moves enough per-example signal that the teacher's training members are detectable from the student alone.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Teacher outputs on transfer data encode member-specific idiosyncrasies (sharper predictions near memorized content), and students fit these idiosyncrasies, so membership of teacher-training images remains detectable from student outputs at levels well above chance even with disjoint transfer sets.

full_record.one_line_idea: Distilled students inherit their teacher's membership secrets: distillation on disjoint transfer data still moves enough per-example signal that the teacher's training members are detectable from the student alone.
full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] Distillation is widely believed to launder privacy: since the student never sees the teacher's training data, releasing only the student is treated as a privacy barrier.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Teacher outputs on transfer data encode member-specific idiosyncrasies (sharper predictions near memorized content), and students fit these idiosyncrasies, so membership of teacher-training images remains detectable from student outputs at levels well above chance even with disjoint transfer sets.
full_record.falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Attacks against students distilled on disjoint public transfer data will achieve membership AUC of at least 0.60 on the teacher's training panel where direct attacks on the teacher achieve at least 0.75, across 2 student capacities; the idea is falsified if student-side AUC falls below 0.55 everywhere, validating distillation as an effective membership barrier.
full_record.why_important: Distillation-as-privacy-laundering is an operating assumption in industrial model release; quantifying leakage through the distillation channel either breaks or certifies a widely used practice.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Distillation privacy has been studied for classifiers in specific settings; the encoder-scale question with disjoint transfer data and quantified leakage retention appears open.
full_record.minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain a teacher with an injected panel, distill students on disjoint data at 2 capacities, and attack students for panel membership with feature- and output-based attacks.
full_record.main_risk: Leakage magnitude likely depends on transfer-set similarity to the teacher corpus; a similarity sweep is needed for the claim to be actionable.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Never-saw-the-data is treated as sufficient for privacy, making distilled releases exempt from pretraining-data scrutiny.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: Student compression may act as an information bottleneck that preferentially discards member-specific idiosyncrasies, genuinely laundering membership.
full_record.fastest_falsification_experiment: 1 teacher pretrain, 2 distillations, plus attacks on public data, one A100: about 5 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Bigger is not leakier at web scale: at fixed unique data, membership risk grows with model size, but along the realistic joint-scaling path (data grows with model) per-image risk falls, inverting the intuitive scale-risk narrative.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-image membership signal increases with capacity at fixed data but decreases with data at fixed capacity (exposure dilution), and along compute-optimal joint scaling the dilution effect dominates, so newer larger releases are less attackable per ordinary image while remaining attackable on the duplicated tail.

full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] Public discussion assumes larger foundation models are automatically worse for privacy, but model releases scale data alongside parameters, and the two effects on per-image exposure act in opposite directions.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-image membership signal increases with capacity at fixed data but decreases with data at fixed capacity (exposure dilution), and along compute-optimal joint scaling the dilution effect dominates, so newer larger releases are less attackable per ordinary image while remaining attackable on the duplicated tail.
full_record.falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In a grid crossing model size with data size, membership AUC will rise with capacity at fixed data (at least +0.05 per 4x capacity) and fall along the joint-scaling diagonal (at least -0.04 per diagonal step) for typical images, while high-duplication images stay flat within 0.03; the idea is falsified if AUC rises along the diagonal for typical images, confirming the bigger-is-leakier narrative.
full_record.why_important: The result determines whether scale is a privacy problem or (with data discipline) a privacy mitigation, directly informing policy debates that currently assume the former.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Capacity and data effects on membership risk are known separately; the joint-scaling-path analysis with duplication stratification appears unmeasured for vision encoders.
full_record.minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a 3x3 model-size by data-size grid, attack each with a fixed strong attack, stratify results by duplication, and read effects along axes and the diagonal.
full_record.main_risk: The diagonal conclusion depends on the assumed joint-scaling policy; results must be reported for at least two plausible scaling paths.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Larger models are assumed monotonically riskier for training-data privacy regardless of accompanying data growth.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: Bigger models may memorize the tail so much more efficiently that even ordinary-image risk rises along realistic scaling paths.
full_record.fastest_falsification_experiment: 9 small pretrains plus attacks on public data, one A100: about 6 GPU-days.

full_record.one_line_idea: Collection-level membership auditing: aggregating weak per-image signals across a photographer's or institution's entire collection yields high-confidence dataset-inclusion tests even when every individual image is undetectable.
full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] Consent and copyright disputes concern collections (a portfolio, a hospital archive, a stock library), but membership tools test single images, where signals on well-generalized encoders are usually too weak for confident claims.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-image membership scores within a collection are weakly positive and nearly independent conditional on data-level covariates, so a covariate-adjusted aggregate test over hundreds of images achieves high power at strict false-positive control, converting useless per-image evidence into a decisive collection-level audit.
full_record.falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] For collections of 300 images where per-image AUC is only 0.55, the aggregate test will detect training inclusion with power at least 0.8 at a 1% false-positive rate against matched non-included collections, and power will scale predictably with collection size; the idea is falsified if achieved power at 1% FPR is under 0.4 for 300-image collections, showing the signals are too correlated or biased to aggregate.
full_record.why_important: This is the statistical instrument that copyright litigation, consent enforcement, and data-governance audits actually need, and it works exactly where per-image inference fails.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Dataset-inference ideas exist for classifiers and language models (Maini et al.); a covariate-adjusted collection-level test with validated FPR control for vision encoders appears missing.
full_record.minimal_falsification_experiment: Train encoders including known collections, compute per-image scores for included and matched excluded collections, form covariate-adjusted aggregate statistics, and estimate power and FPR by resampling.
full_record.main_risk: Collections share style covariates that could inflate false positives on excluded-but-similar collections; the matched-control design carries the burden of the result.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Membership inference on well-trained encoders is dismissed as too weak for real-world evidentiary use.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: Within-collection score correlations (shared style, camera, subject) may slash the effective sample size, making the aggregate barely stronger than one image.

one_line_idea: Reported membership-inference success on vision foundation models is inflated by member/non-member distribution mismatch: attacks are partly detecting which crawl an image came from, not whether the model saw it.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A substantial fraction of reported attack AUC against vision encoders is explained by distributional cues (vintage, resolution statistics, site style) that a classifier could detect without any access to the target model, and temporally and stylistically matched re-evaluation collapses much of the claimed success.

full_record.one_line_idea: Reported membership-inference success on vision foundation models is inflated by member/non-member distribution mismatch: attacks are partly detecting which crawl an image came from, not whether the model saw it.
full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] Public membership evaluations against foundation encoders assemble member sets from known training corpora and non-member sets from elsewhere (newer crawls, different sites), so the two pools differ in ways unrelated to training.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A substantial fraction of reported attack AUC against vision encoders is explained by distributional cues (vintage, resolution statistics, site style) that a classifier could detect without any access to the target model, and temporally and stylistically matched re-evaluation collapses much of the claimed success.
full_record.falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A model-free classifier trained to distinguish member from non-member pools using image statistics alone will achieve at least half of the published attack's AUC excess over 0.5 on at least 2 public evaluation setups, and matched-pool re-evaluation will cut attack AUC excess by at least 40%; the idea is falsified if the model-free classifier stays near 0.5 (under 0.55) and matched re-evaluation changes AUC by under 10% relative.
full_record.why_important: Both privacy alarm and privacy complacency are being anchored to numbers that may measure crawl provenance; correcting the protocol changes the evidentiary value of every such audit.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Distribution-mismatch critiques of membership evaluation exist in the security literature; a quantified decomposition for vision foundation-model audits appears missing.
full_record.minimal_falsification_experiment: Reproduce 2 public encoder membership evaluations, train model-free pool classifiers on image statistics, construct matched pools via stratified resampling, and compare attack AUCs before and after matching.
full_record.main_risk: Truly matched non-member pools are hard to construct for models trained on near-exhaustive crawls, potentially leaving residual mismatch in both directions.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Published membership AUCs on foundation models are taken at face value as measurements of model leakage.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: Careful existing evaluations may already control provenance well enough that the model-free classifier finds nothing, vindicating current numbers.
full_record.fastest_falsification_experiment: Analysis plus re-evaluation using existing public checkpoints and public image pools, one A100: about 2 GPU-days; no pretraining required.

one_line_idea: Better encoders are more invertible: input-image reconstructability from frozen patch tokens increases with encoder scale, contradicting the intuition that more abstract features are safer to share.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Scale improves the information efficiency of features: larger encoders preserve more input-specific detail in linearly accessible form, so reconstruction attacks against frozen patch tokens recover inputs with fidelity that increases, not decreases, along scale ladders at fixed token count.

full_record.one_line_idea: Better encoders are more invertible: input-image reconstructability from frozen patch tokens increases with encoder scale, contradicting the intuition that more abstract features are safer to share.
full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] Organizations share dense features (patch tokens, feature maps) across services and vendors on the assumption that features abstract away pixel content, and that stronger models abstract more.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Scale improves the information efficiency of features: larger encoders preserve more input-specific detail in linearly accessible form, so reconstruction attacks against frozen patch tokens recover inputs with fidelity that increases, not decreases, along scale ladders at fixed token count.
full_record.falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Training identical reconstruction decoders against patch tokens from a 4-rung public encoder ladder will show monotone fidelity improvement with scale, with the largest rung beating the smallest by at least 0.1 LPIPS (or 20% relative retrieval-based identification), and the idea is falsified if fidelity is flat within 0.03 LPIPS or decreases with scale.
full_record.why_important: Feature-sharing practices and privacy reviews assume an abstraction gradient that this result would invert: the better the model you buy, the more your shared features reveal.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Feature inversion is classical (Mahendran-Vedaldi, Dosovitskiy-Brox era) on individual networks; the scale-trend claim across modern foundation ladders appears unmeasured.
full_record.minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix a reconstruction decoder architecture and training budget, train one per ladder rung against frozen tokens on public images, and evaluate reconstruction fidelity and identification rate on held-out images.
full_record.main_risk: Fidelity differences may be driven by token dimensionality rather than scale per se, requiring dimension-matched controls via random projection.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Stronger encoders are assumed to produce more abstract, less pixel-revealing features, making feature sharing safer as models improve.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: Heavy augmentation in large-model training might genuinely discard instance detail, flattening or reversing the invertibility trend.
full_record.fastest_falsification_experiment: 4 decoder trainings against public checkpoints on public images, one A100: about 3 GPU-days.

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Modern foundation embeddings preserve identity- and location-linking information so well that nearest-neighbor search over an attacker's gallery re-identifies the subject or place of an embedded photo at high rates, and linkage success scales with both embedding model quality and gallery size along measurable curves.

full_record.one_line_idea: Global embeddings re-identify: a single CLIP-style image vector suffices to link a person or place across photo collections at rates that make embedding release equivalent to content release for linkage purposes.
full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] Image embeddings are stored, shared, and sold at scale (search indices, recommendation systems, analytics) under the assumption that a vector is not personal data in the way the photo is.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Modern foundation embeddings preserve identity- and location-linking information so well that nearest-neighbor search over an attacker's gallery re-identifies the subject or place of an embedded photo at high rates, and linkage success scales with both embedding model quality and gallery size along measurable curves.
full_record.falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Given only a global embedding of a held-out photo and a 1M-image public gallery, subject/place linkage (same person or same specific location retrieved in top-10) will succeed for at least 30% of photos of repeatedly photographed subjects, rising with gallery coverage; the idea is falsified if linkage stays under 10% even for well-covered subjects, showing global pooling destroys linkage signal.
full_record.why_important: Data-protection frameworks currently treat embeddings ambiguously; measured linkage curves would ground the legal and engineering debate about whether vectors are personal data in the operative sense.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Embedding-search linkage is obvious to practitioners; a systematic linkage-rate curve versus model scale and gallery coverage framed as a privacy measurement appears unpublished.
full_record.minimal_falsification_experiment: Embed held-out photos of subjects with known repeated appearances in a public gallery, run nearest-neighbor linkage across embedding models of increasing scale, and fit linkage-rate curves versus gallery coverage.
full_record.main_risk: Linkage rates depend heavily on subject distinctiveness; results must be stratified (landmarks versus persons versus interiors) to avoid one stratum dominating the headline.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Storing embeddings instead of images is widely treated as a meaningful privacy mitigation.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: For non-famous subjects with sparse galleries, linkage may be so rare that embeddings are effectively safe in realistic threat models.
full_record.fastest_falsification_experiment: Embedding and retrieval over public galleries with existing checkpoints, one A100: about 1-2 GPU-days; no training required.

one_line_idea: Redact-then-encode fails: content masked out of an image before encoding is partially recoverable from the visible-region tokens, because attention mixes neighborhood evidence into every token, and the leak grows with encoder scale.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Visible-region tokens absorb contextual inferences about redacted content (who plausibly stood there, what the screen likely showed at category level), so attribute-recovery attacks on redacted-region content succeed above chance using only visible-region tokens, with success growing with encoder scale and context strength.

full_record.one_line_idea: Redact-then-encode fails: content masked out of an image before encoding is partially recoverable from the visible-region tokens, because attention mixes neighborhood evidence into every token, and the leak grows with encoder scale.
full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] Privacy pipelines blur or blackout sensitive regions (faces, plates, screens) before running foundation encoders, treating the redaction as final; token-level information flow in ViTs is not part of that threat model.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Visible-region tokens absorb contextual inferences about redacted content (who plausibly stood there, what the screen likely showed at category level), so attribute-recovery attacks on redacted-region content succeed above chance using only visible-region tokens, with success growing with encoder scale and context strength.
full_record.falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Attribute classifiers reading only visible-region tokens of redacted images will recover redacted-region attributes (clothing color, object category, coarse identity group) at least 15 points above chance on average across attributes, and at least 5 points above a pixels-only baseline given the same visible pixels; the idea is falsified if token-based recovery is within 2 points of the pixel baseline, showing encoders add no contextual amplification.
full_record.why_important: If encoders amplify contextual leakage beyond what the visible pixels imply, redaction standards for pipelines that share features (not images) are systematically insufficient and need feature-side controls.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Attention mixing is well known mechanically; its quantification as a redaction-defeating leakage channel with pixel-baseline controls appears missing.
full_record.minimal_falsification_experiment: Redact annotated regions on public images, encode with ladder encoders, train attribute probes on visible-region tokens versus visible-pixel baselines, and compare recovery rates across scales.
full_record.main_risk: The pixel baseline must be strong (same architecture retrained on redacted pixels) or the encoder amplification claim is confounded by probe capacity.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Redaction before encoding is treated as removing the redacted information from all downstream artifacts.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: Encoders may add little beyond what strong pixel-context models already infer, making the redaction gap a property of context, not of encoding.
full_record.fastest_falsification_experiment: Probe training over public checkpoints on redacted public images, one A100: about 2-3 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Dense features are location beacons: mid-layer features of general-purpose encoders support geolocation of ordinary photos far above prior-based baselines, and pretraining data scale drives the effect.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Web-scale pretraining embeds fine-grained place signatures (vegetation, architecture, signage statistics, road furniture) into general features, so lightweight probes on shared dense features geolocate ordinary non-landmark photos to country and region far above population priors, with accuracy scaling with pretraining data size.

full_record.one_line_idea: Dense features are location beacons: mid-layer features of general-purpose encoders support geolocation of ordinary photos far above prior-based baselines, and pretraining data scale drives the effect.
full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] Geolocation from images is treated as a specialized capability of dedicated models, and feature-sharing risk assessments do not include location inference among the leaked attributes of general encoder features.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Web-scale pretraining embeds fine-grained place signatures (vegetation, architecture, signage statistics, road furniture) into general features, so lightweight probes on shared dense features geolocate ordinary non-landmark photos to country and region far above population priors, with accuracy scaling with pretraining data size.
full_record.falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Probes on frozen features of a data-scale encoder ladder will localize held-out non-landmark photos to the correct country at least 2.5x the prior-based baseline, improving monotonically with pretraining data over a 10x range; the idea is falsified if feature-based geolocation stays under 1.3x prior baseline or shows no data-scale trend.
full_record.why_important: It adds a concrete, testable attribute-leakage channel (location) to the privacy accounting of every feature-sharing pipeline, with the scaling result forecasting that the channel widens as corpora grow.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Dedicated geolocation models exist; quantifying incidental geolocation capability of general encoder features as a function of pretraining data scale appears unstudied.
full_record.minimal_falsification_experiment: Train geolocation probes on frozen features from encoders pretrained at nested data scales, evaluate on public geo-tagged non-landmark photos, and compare against priors and pixel-baseline models.
full_record.main_risk: Geo-tagged evaluation photos skew toward tourist content; careful non-landmark filtering is required for the ordinary photo claim.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Location inference is considered a capability of specialized systems, not a latent property of shared general-purpose features.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: Country-level cues may be learnable from modest data with no further scale trend, making the channel real but scale-static.
full_record.fastest_falsification_experiment: Probe training over public checkpoints and geo-tagged public data, one A100: about 2 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: A measured privacy-utility frontier for feature release: quantization, dimension reduction, and token pooling cut inversion and linkage risk at quantified utility costs, yielding a publishable recipe instead of folklore.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Across standard transformations, inversion and linkage attacks degrade much faster than downstream utility over a wide operating range because attacks depend on fragile high-frequency feature detail while utility rides on robust coarse structure, so the frontier contains deep near-free privacy regions and identifiable best-per-budget recipes.

full_record.one_line_idea: A measured privacy-utility frontier for feature release: quantization, dimension reduction, and token pooling cut inversion and linkage risk at quantified utility costs, yielding a publishable recipe instead of folklore.
full_record.problem: [KNOWN FACT] Teams that must share features apply ad hoc transformations (PCA, quantization, pooling) hoping to reduce risk, with no quantitative map from transformation strength to attack degradation and utility loss.
full_record.core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Across standard transformations, inversion and linkage attacks degrade much faster than downstream utility over a wide operating range because attacks depend on fragile high-frequency feature detail while utility rides on robust coarse structure, so the frontier contains deep near-free privacy regions and identifiable best-per-budget recipes.
full_record.falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Mapping 3 transformation families at 5 strengths each will find operating points cutting reconstruction fidelity by at least 50% relative and linkage top-10 rate by at least 60% relative while losing under 2% relative on a fixed utility suite; the idea is falsified if every point that achieves those attack reductions costs over 8% relative utility, showing attacks and utility degrade together.
full_record.why_important: Feature sharing is ubiquitous and unavoidable in production systems; a validated frontier converts privacy engineering for features from guesswork into a lookup.
full_record.why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual defenses are studied against single attacks; a joint frontier across transformation families, attack types, and utility suites for modern foundation features appears unassembled.
full_record.minimal_falsification_experiment: For 2 public encoders, apply the transformation grid to features, run inversion and linkage attacks plus a downstream utility suite per cell, and assemble the three-axis frontier.
full_record.main_risk: Adaptive attackers who fine-tune attacks per transformation may close the frontier gap; the map must include adaptive re-attack for headline points.
full_record.community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Feature transformations are assumed to trade utility for privacy roughly linearly, so aggressive protection is presumed expensive.
full_record.why_it_might_be_wrong: For linkage (as opposed to inversion), coarse structure may be exactly what attacks use, collapsing the near-free region for the attack that matters most.
full_record.fastest_falsification_experiment: Attack and probe grid over transformed features of public checkpoints, one A100: about 4 GPU-days; no pretraining.
